title: Holi: the festival of colors
hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
carry: the name of god outlasts the fire
tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali, a prison thrown open and lamps before dawn. From darkness, lead me to light.

A street in north India, on a spring morning. Somebody's uncle is purple. A grandmother is laughing with green powder in her hair. A stranger you've never met walks up, says happy Holi, and smears pink on your cheek, and you do the same back. Water balloons from a balcony. Drums from somewhere. By noon you can't tell the banker from the delivery driver, or the neighbor you haven't spoken to in a year from your own cousin. Everyone is the same muddy, glorious color. But the night before, there was a fire, and the fire is where the story is.
screen: `A STRANGER SMEARS PINK ON YOUR CHEEK.` → `NOBODY CAN TELL WHO IS WHO.` → `BUT FIRST, A FIRE.`

segments.voice: The story is about a boy named Prahlad. His father, Hiranyakashipu, is a demon king with a boon that makes him nearly impossible to kill, and he decides that makes him God. Everyone in the kingdom must worship him. His own son won't. Prahlad keeps saying the name of Vishnu. The Bhagavata Purana tells how his father tries everything: snakes, elephants, a cliff, poison. The boy survives each one. Then comes the part the festival remembers. The king's sister, Holika, is said to be protected from fire. She takes Prahlad on her lap and sits down in a blazing pyre. And the fire turns. Holika burns. The boy walks out unharmed, still saying the name. An honest note: the Bhagavata tells Prahlad's story and ends it with Narasimha; the Holika scene comes from later tellings and the festival itself. Either way, the heart is the same, and it's one of Hinduism's most loved practices: the Name. Repeating God's name, called japa, or singing it together, kirtan. Prahlad had no army, only the name, and in the story it was enough. So on the full-moon night of Phalguna, at the end of winter, people light bonfires called Holika Dahan, and many walk around them, remembering a fire that couldn't hold a child. The next morning, the colors. People say it with a grin: bura na mano, Holi hai. Don't be offended, it's Holi. For one day the lines between people get smudged on purpose, and old quarrels are supposed to end. Holi has other stories too, and i'll come back for them.
screen: `A BOY WHO KEEPS SAYING THE NAME.` · `HOLIKA SITS IN THE FIRE.` · `JAPA: REPEATING GOD'S NAME.` · `THE BONFIRE THE NIGHT BEFORE.` · then, large: `THE NAME OF GOD OUTLASTS THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: Choose a name of God: Hari, Rama, Krishna, Shiva, or simply Ma. Say it slowly, eleven times, out loud or inside, counting on your fingers, the way Prahlad kept saying his. Think of a place where saying what you believe feels hard. If you don't pray, choose one word that holds what you stand for. Then picture tomorrow's colors, and one person you'd smudge first, to make up.
Holi. The spring festival of colors, the morning after the bonfire that remembers Prahlad walking out of the fire.
Your line: the name of god outlasts the fire. Prahlad had only the name, and it was enough. That's day eighty-two.

Hiranyakashipu.meaning: Prahlad's father, a demon king who demanded worship

Holika.meaning: the king's sister, said to be protected from fire

Narasimha.meaning: Vishnu appearing as half man, half lion

Phalguna.meaning: the month at winter's end when Holi falls

japa.meaning: repeating a name of God, often counted on beads
